focus: Mode registry, graph policy compilation, canonical identities, capability ceilings, and migration boundaries
noveltyJustification: 3 of 7 findings are fully new semantic-projection, ownership, and migration decisions and 4 are partially new registry, alias, compilation, and identity mappings: (3 + 0.5 * 4) / 7 = 0.714, rounded to 0.71.
keyQuestions: How should organization graph policy, admission, gate kinds, executor capabilities, and graph resource classes consume the mode registry without turning routing metadata or aliases into authority?
answeredQuestions: The ownership matrix, authority-relevant registry projection, compilation flow, tenant/role scope, alias and rename behavior, audit provenance, compatibility, mutants, and non-applicability are decided at design level.
ruledOut: Putting tenant policy, roles, gate outcomes, or verdicts in mode-registry metadata
Matching policy against aliases, commands, packets, agents, or instance names
Treating toolSurface or executor self-report as request authority
Allowing organization policy to widen platform or mode ceilings
Lowering ASK to ALLOW without durable gate evidence and fresh 036 reevaluation
Rewriting historical canonical modes through aliases

summary: The mode registry owns canonical routing identity and maximum tool surfaces, not tenant governance, admission, gates, current authorization, or effects.
Compiled graph policy captures a canonical authority-relevant projection of mode/backend/tool fields while full registry identity remains audit provenance and aliases remain routing-only.
Only exact canonical workflowMode enters policy, admission, evidence, and authorization; aliases, commands, packets, agents, and instance names grant nothing.
Admission owns sealed executable kinds and required classes while trusted runtime evidence owns actual executor capabilities; mode toolSurface remains only one upper bound.
Compilation preserves deny-ask-allow precedence and source provenance; ASK opens a durable gate and only fresh 036 reevaluation can authorize.
Organization policy and trusted identity evidence own tenants and roles; mode and agent labels cannot authenticate a principal or satisfy an approver role.
Authority-relevant projection drift forces policy and admission recompilation, while aliases remain routing compatibility and never rewrite stored canonical identities.
